nameStory: This golden beauty gets its unusual name from the bright yellow robes once worn by papal clerks called 'prothonotaries' in the Roman Catholic Church. When early naturalists saw this warbler's brilliant yellow-orange head and chest, they thought it looked just like those ceremonial vestments!
description: The Prothonotary Warbler is a small, stocky songbird about the size of a chickadee, measuring roughly 5 inches long. Males are absolutely stunning with their brilliant golden-yellow heads and underparts that seem to glow in dappled sunlight, contrasting sharply with blue-gray wings and white undertail feathers. Females are similar but with more muted yellow tones. This is one of the most colorful warblers you'll see in New England's wetlands.

idTips.label: Golden glow
idTips.description: The male's head and chest shine like a golden beacon - so bright yellow-orange it almost seems to emit its own light in shadowy swamps

idTips.label: Blue-gray wings
idTips.description: Wings and back are distinctly blue-gray, creating a striking contrast against the golden body that catches your eye immediately

idTips.label: Jerky movements
idTips.description: Moves with quick, twitchy motions and will even crawl upside down on branches like a tiny acrobat - very different from other warblers

idTips.label: White undertail
idTips.description: Flashes bright white patches under the tail when flying or hopping - visible even from a distance

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: Noticeably stockier and rounder than most warblers, with a proportionally larger head and shorter tail

idTips.label: Cavity nesting behavior
idTips.description: Often seen investigating tree holes, nest boxes, or old woodpecker cavities - the only eastern warbler that nests in cavities

habitat: Look for Prothonotary Warblers in wooded swamps, beaver ponds, and forested wetlands where standing or slow-moving water meets mature trees. They prefer areas with dead trees (snags) or nest boxes near water, as they need cavities for nesting. In New England, they're most often found in river bottomlands and edges of wooded ponds.

seasonality.spring: Males arrive in late April to early May and are most vocal then, singing persistently from prominent perches while establishing territory and seeking mates near wetland nesting sites.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity as pairs raise young in tree cavities. Adults are busy gathering insects and can be seen making frequent trips to and from nest holes.
seasonality.fall: Birds become quieter and less conspicuous as they prepare for migration in August and September. Young birds lack the intense golden coloring of adults.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England - these birds migrate to Central and South America, spending winter in tropical mangrove swamps and coastal forests.

funFact: Prothonotary Warblers are one of only two warbler species that nest in cavities, and they're so particular about it that they'll sometimes evict other birds from perfect nest holes, then line the cavity with moss so thick and soft you could use it as a pillow!
confusionNotes: The brilliant golden color might remind you of a goldfinch, but goldfinches have black wings and are seed-eaters found in open areas, while Prothonotary Warblers have blue-gray wings and stick to wooded swamps. Remember: 'Golden in the swamp = Prothonotary, golden in the field = goldfinch.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'warbler,' this bird's scientific name 'citrea' means 'of citrus,' referring to its lemon-yellow coloring. The species gained historical fame when it was mentioned during the Alger Hiss espionage trial in 1948, as birdwatching became an unexpected piece of evidence!
compareHints: As the only member of its genus, the Prothonotary Warbler is unique among eastern warblers for its cavity-nesting behavior. Compared to other yellow warblers in its family like Yellow Warblers or American Goldfinches, it's much more golden-orange rather than pure yellow, has distinctive blue-gray wings, and is exclusively found near water in wooded swamps rather than open areas or dry forests.
